verses.text: “Do you know the time when the mountain goats give birth? Do you watch when the doe bears fawns?
Can you count the months that they fulfill? Or do you know the time when they give birth?
They bow themselves, they bear their young. They end their labor pains.
Their young ones become strong. They grow up in the open field. They go out, and don’t return again.
“Who has set the wild donkey free? Or who has loosened the bonds of the swift donkey,
Whose home I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling place?
He scorns the tumult of the city, neither does he hear the shouting of the driver.
The range of the mountains is his pasture, He searches after every green thing.
“Will the wild ox be content to serve you? Or will he stay by your feeding trough?
Can you hold the wild ox in the furrow with his harness? Or will he till the valleys after you?
Will you trust him, because his strength is great? Or will you leave to him your labor?
Will you confide in him, that he will bring home your seed, and gather the grain of your threshing floor?
“The wings of the ostrich wave proudly; but are they the feathers and plumage of love?
For she leaves her eggs on the earth, warms them in the dust,
and forgets that the foot may crush them, or that the wild animal may trample them.
She deals harshly with her young ones, as if they were not hers. Though her labor is in vain, she is without fear,
because God has deprived her of wisdom, neither has he imparted to her understanding.
When she lifts up herself on high, she scorns the horse and his rider.
“Have you given the horse might? Have you clothed his neck with a quivering mane?
Have you made him to leap as a locust? The glory of his snorting is awesome.
He paws in the valley, and rejoices in his strength. He goes out to meet the armed men.
He mocks at fear, and is not dismayed, neither does he turn back from the sword.
The quiver rattles against him, the flashing spear and the javelin.
He eats up the ground with fierceness and rage, neither does he stand still at the sound of the trumpet.
As often as the trumpet sounds he snorts, ‘Aha!’ He smells the battle afar off, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting.
“Is it by your wisdom that the hawk soars, and stretches her wings toward the south?
Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up, and makes his nest on high?
On the cliff he dwells, and makes his home, on the point of the cliff, and the stronghold.
From there he spies out the prey. His eyes see it afar off.
His young ones also suck up blood. Where the slain are, there he is.”

footnotes.content: The Lord asks Job a question he cannot answer: when the mountain goat gives birth, who watches? It's a gentle rebuke—Job has spent so many words on his own suffering, but he's never witnessed the hidden kindnesses the Lord shows in the wilderness. The Lord keeps company with the doe bearing her fawns, and we are not forgotten either.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Can you count the months? Can you know the time? Job cannot. But the Lord knows—He keeps the calendar of every creature's season, every birth, every beginning. There is a patience in that knowing, a tenderness that doesn't rush. When we feel forgotten in our waiting, it helps to remember that the Lord counts even the days of the wild animals He loves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bow themselves and bear their young; their labor pains end. So simple, and yet—what strength it takes, and what wisdom is built into the body. The Lord has not left creation to guess at this; He has woven provision into the very creature. When we bow under our own burdens, He is already working to bring us through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The young ones grow strong in the open field and go out, never to return to their mother again. It's hard to read—a kind of letting go. Yet the Lord sends them forth with strength He has given them. Sometimes He asks the same of us: to trust that He has made us ready for the open field, and that release itself is His care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wild donkey has been set free—there is no hand that enslaved him into freedom. The Lord Himself is the one who did this. How often do we forget that true liberty comes not from our own breaking of chains, but from the kindness of the One who loosens them? We are free because He has chosen it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wilderness is his home; the salt land his dwelling. Not a prison, but a gift—the Lord has made a place for him and given him a domain. Even in barrenness, there is purpose. Job feels cast out into his own wilderness of suffering, but the Lord is showing him: I make homes even in hard places, and I am Lord there too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He scorns the tumult of the city and does not hear the driver's shout. There is a freedom in this indifference—the wild donkey is not governed by human clamor or command. Sometimes the deepest peace comes when we, like him, refuse to let the world's noise master our hearts. The Lord keeps a place for those who will not be enslaved by the shouting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mountains are his pasture; he searches for every green thing. He is not idle—he seeks, he roams, he lives. The Lord has made a creature not at rest in despair, but seeking. When we are tempted to give up and sit still in our grief, the wild donkey reminds us: there is always another mountain to climb, always some green thing the Lord has hidden for us to find.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Will the wild ox be content to serve you? The answer is no—and the Lord seems pleased by it. Not every creature is meant to bow to human will; some are made to resist, to be strong in their refusal. Job is learning that the world is not his to command. Humility begins when we stop asking the ox to serve and start asking the Lord to teach us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Can you hold the wild ox in the furrow with his harness? Job cannot—and neither can we. The Lord is reminding him that some things are not ours to control, no matter how we try to bind them. This speaks to anyone who has held too tightly, demanded too much, tried to harness what belongs only to God. Release begins with seeing what you never owned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Will you trust him because his strength is great? The irony cuts deep—Job cannot even trust himself with his own strength, let alone the wild ox. Trust requires surrender, a ceasing of control. The Lord asks: can you trust Me, whose strength is not great but infinite? That is the lesson hidden in this question about the ox.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Will he bring home your seed? Will he gather your grain? No, he will not—he is not made for your purposes. But the Lord is reminding Job that the gathering of the harvest is not ultimately his work either. We plant and water; the Lord gives the increase. We are more like the wild ox than we imagine—not the masters of our own productivity, but workers in a harvest we do not control.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ostrich waves her wings proudly—but are they the feathers of love? There is something almost sad in this question. Beauty and strength are not the same as affection; capability is not kindness. Job has been strong, proud even, but his strength has not saved him. The Lord seems to ask: when all your feathers fall away, what will be left?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She leaves her eggs on the earth, warms them in the dust. The ostrich makes no elaborate nest; she is raw and simple in her mothering. There is something vulnerable in this—eggs left in the dust seem so exposed, so fragile. Yet the Lord entrusts His creatures to such humble care, and they survive. Sometimes the plainest love is the truest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She forgets that a foot may crush her eggs or a wild animal trample them. The ostrich doesn't worry—she simply trusts. Job has worried enough for himself and the whole world, yet here is a creature who lays everything down without anxiety. Is the Lord whispering: trust with her simplicity? The outcome is in My hands, not yours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She deals harshly with her young ones, as if they were not hers; her labor is in vain, yet she is without fear. The ostrich mother is cruel by human standards, yet the Lord counts her as part of His order. It's a hard saying—not every creature mothers the way we think she should. Perhaps the Lord is saying to Job: I work in ways that seem strange to you, and yet they are right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God has deprived her of wisdom; He has not imparted understanding to her. The ostrich acts on instinct alone, without reason—and yet she survives. This seems to overturn everything we value: intelligence, planning, foresight. The Lord is teaching Job that wisdom as humans measure it is not the only kind of wisdom. Sometimes faith alone is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When she lifts herself up on high, she scorns the horse and his rider. Here is the point: the ostrich, lacking human wisdom, is yet unafraid. She scorns what humans think is mighty. The Lord gives her a kind of nobility that has nothing to do with reason or calculation. Job, with all his understanding, has lost this simple courage. The Lord offers to teach him back to it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Have you given the horse might? Have you clothed his neck with a quivering mane? The Lord now speaks of the warhorse, made for strength and glory. But the question is not about the horse alone—it is about the Lord's generosity. Every good thing, every source of strength and beauty, comes from His hand. Job's hands have grown empty; the Lord reminds him: I am the giver of all gifts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The horse leaps like a locust; his snorting is awesome in its glory. There is something almost joyful here—the Lord delights in describing this creature's power and beauty. He is showing Job: I make beautiful things for their own sake, not for human use alone. In your suffering, you have forgotten how to see beauty simply as a sign of My generosity and pleasure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He paws in the valley and rejoices in his strength; he goes out to meet the armed men. The warhorse does not shrink from battle—he runs toward it with joy. He has been made for this, and he knows it. Job has lost his way, but the warhorse is true to his nature. The Lord asks: will you return to yours? I made you for more than you remember.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He mocks at fear and is not dismayed; he does not turn back from the sword. The horse has no choice but to trust his maker and run forward. There is a lesson in this for Job's spiritual warfare: to mock fear, to stand firm, to never turn back from what the Lord calls us toward. Courage is not the absence of danger but the refusal to let it master you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The quiver rattles against him; the flashing spear and javelin surround him. Yet he runs on. The horse is not protected from the weapons of war—he runs into them with eyes open. Sometimes the Lord's call is not to safety but to faithful obedience despite the danger. Job has thought his suffering means the Lord has abandoned him; here the horse shows him: sometimes the hardest path is the truest one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He eats up the ground with fierceness and rage; he does not stand still at the trumpet's sound. The horse's power is not gentle—it is fierce and relentless. The Lord is showing Job that strength is sometimes meant to be fierce, that we are not always called to passivity or resignation. Trust the Lord's design in you, even when it feels wild.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As often as the trumpet sounds, he snorts 'Aha!'; he smells the battle afar off. The horse hears the call to war and responds with eagerness. He recognizes his calling from a distance. Job, too, has been called to something—perhaps not to battle, but to trust and to witness the Lord's wisdom. The question is: will Job respond to that call with the horse's eagerness?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Is it by your wisdom that the hawk soars and stretches her wings toward the south? Job has not taught the hawk to fly; he does not know the winds and currents by which she soars. Yet the hawk soars faithfully, season after season. The Lord is asking: do you trust Me as the hawk trusts the air beneath her wings? That is the wisdom the hawk knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up and makes his nest on high? The eagle chooses the cliff, the stronghold, not because Job has ordered him but because the Lord has written it into his nature. We, too, are drawn toward what the Lord has placed in us. Job's calling is written in his heart; the pain has not erased it. The Lord is asking: will you climb again?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the cliff he dwells; on the point of the cliff is his stronghold. The eagle builds his home in the most precarious place, yet he is safe there. It seems like madness from below, but from his vantage point, the cliff is the safest place. Job feels cast onto a cliff, but the Lord suggests: this is where you are meant to see Me. Perspective changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From there he spies out the prey; his eyes see it afar off. The eagle sees far and wide from his high place—he has vision. Suffering can sharpen our sight, give us eyes to see the Lord's hand where we might have been blind before. Job will not understand this until the end, but the Lord is suggesting: your pain has given you a cliff to stand on. What can you see from here that others cannot?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His young ones suck up blood; where the slain are, there he is. Readers today hear an echo: even in places of death, the Lord sustains life. The eagle feeds on what falls, transforms it into nourishment for his young. As of 2026-10, we have learned this hard lesson well—that the Lord wastes nothing, redeems everything, and can bring life from the places we thought only held ending.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
